passage_6.text:
Time and again, whenever a population [of Mexican tetra fish] was swept into a cave and survived long enough for natural selection to have its way, the eyes disappeared. "But it's not that everything has been lost in cavefish . . . Many enhancements have also happened." . . . Studies have found that cave-dwelling fish can detect lower levels of amino acids than surface fish can. They also have more tastebuds and a higher density of sensitive cells alongside their bodies that let them sense water pressure and flow. . . .

Killing the processes that support the formation of the eye is quite literally what happens. Just like non-cave-dwelling members of the species, all cavefish embryos start making eyes. But after a few hours, cells in the developing eye start dying, until the entire structure has disappeared. [Developmental biologist Misty] Riddle thinks this apparent inefficiency may be unavoidable. "The early development of the brain and the eye are completely intertwined-they happen together," she says. That means the least disruptive way for eyelessness to evolve may be to start making an eye and then get rid of it. . . .

It's easy to see why cavefish would be at a disadvantage if they were to maintain expensive tissues they aren't using. Since relatively little lives or grows in their caves, the fish are likely surviving on a meager diet of mostly bat feces and organic waste that washes in during the rainy season. Researchers keeping cavefish in labs have discovered that, genetically, the creatures are exquisitely adapted to absorbing and storing nutrients. . . .

Fats can be toxic for tissues, [evolutionary physiologist Nicolas] Rohner explains, so they are stored in fat cells. "But when these cells get too big, they can burst, which is why we often see chronic inflammation in humans and other animals that have stored a lot of fat in their tissues." Yet a 2020 study by Rohner, Krishnan and their colleagues revealed that even very well-fed cavefish had fewer signs of inflammation in their fat tissues than surface fish do. Even in their sparse cave conditions, wild cavefish can sometimes get very fat, says Riddle. This is presumably because, whenever food ends up in the cave, the fish eat as much of it as possible, since there may be nothing else for a long time to come. Intriguingly, Riddle says, their fat is usually bright yellow, because of high levels of carotenoids, the substance in the carrots that your grandmother used to tell you were good for your...eyes.

"The first thing that came to our mind, of course, was that they were accumulating these because they don't have eyes," says Riddle. In this species, such ideas can be tested: Scientists can cross surface fish (with eyes) and cavefish (without eyes) and look at what their offspring are like. When that's done, Riddle says, researchers see no link between eye presence or size and the accumulation of carotenoids. Some eyeless cavefish had fat that was practically white, indicating lower carotenoid levels. Instead, Riddle thinks these carotenoids may be another adaptation to suppress inflammation, which might be important in the wild, as cavefish are likely overeating whenever food arrives.

passage_10.text:
This book takes the position that setting in literature is more than just backdrop, that important insight into literary texts can be made by paying close attention to how authors craft place, as well as to how place functions in a narrative. The authors included in this reference work engage deeply with either real or imagined geographies. They care about how human decisions have shaped landscapes and how landscapes have shaped human practices and values. Some of the best writing is highly vivid, employing the language of the senses because this is the primary means through which humans know physical space.

Literature can offer valuable perspectives on physical and cultural geography. Unlike scientific reports, a literary narrative can provide the emotional component missing from the scientific record. In human experience, geographical places have a spiritual or emotional component in addition to and as part of a physical layout and topography. This emotional component, although subjective, is no less "real" than a surveyor's map. Human consciousness of place is experienced in a multi-modal manner. Histories of places live on in many forms, one of which is the human memory or imagination.

Both real and imaginary landscapes provide insight into the human experience of place. The pursuit of such a topic speaks to the valuable knowledge produced from bridging disciplines and combining material from both the arts and the sciences to better understand the human condition. The perspectives that most concern cultural geographers are often those regarding movement and migration, cultivation of natural resources, and organization of space. The latter two reflect concerns of the built environment, a topic shared with the field of architectural study. Many of these concerns are also reflected in work sociologists do. Scholars from literary studies can contribute an aesthetic dimension to what might otherwise be a purely ideological approach.

Literature can bring together material that spans different branches of science. For example, a literary description of place may involve not only the environment and geography but the noises and quality of light, or how people from different races or classes can experience the same place in different ways linked to those racial or class disparities. Literary texts can also account for the way in which absence-of other people, animals, and so on-affects a human observer or inhabitant. Both literary and scientific approaches to place are necessary, working in unison, to achieve a complete record of an environment. It is important to note that the interdisciplinary nature of this work teaches us that landscapes are not static, that they are not unchanged by human culture. At least part of their identity derives from the people who inhabit them and from the way space can alter and inspire human perspective. The intersection of scientific and literary expression that happens in the study of literary geography is of prime importance due to the complexity of the personal and political ways that humans experience place.

passage_11.text:
In [my book "Searches"], I chronicle how big technology companies have exploited human language for their gain. We let this happen, I argue, because we also benefit somewhat from using the products. It's a dynamic that makes us complicit in big tech's accumulation of wealth and power: we're both victims and beneficiaries. I describe this complicity, but I also enact it, through my own internet archives: my Google searches, my Amazon product reviews and, yes, my ChatGPT dialogues. . . .

People often describe chatbots' textual output as "bland" or "generic" - the linguistic equivalent of a beige office building. OpenAI's products are built to "sound like a colleague", as OpenAI puts it, using language that, coming from a person, would sound "polite", "empathetic", "kind", "rationally optimistic" and "engaging", among other qualities. OpenAI describes these strategies as helping its products seem "professional" and "approachable". This appears to be bound up with making us feel safe . . .

Trust is a challenge for artificial intelligence (AI) companies, partly because their products regularly produce falsehoods and reify sexist, racist, US-centric cultural norms. While the companies are working on these problems, they persist: OpenAI found that its latest systems generate errors at a higher rate than its previous system. In the book, I wrote about the inaccuracies and biases and also demonstrated them with the products. When I prompted Microsoft's Bing Image Creator to produce a picture of engineers and space explorers, it gave me an entirely male cast of characters; when my father asked ChatGPT to edit his writing, it transmuted his perfectly correct Indian English into American English. Those weren't flukes. Research suggests that both tendencies are widespread.

In my own ChatGPT dialogues, I wanted to enact how the product's veneer of collegial neutrality could lull us into absorbing false or biased responses without much critical engagement. Over time, ChatGPT seemed to be guiding me to write a more positive book about big tech - including editing my description of OpenAI's CEO, Sam Altman, to call him "a visionary and a pragmatist". I'm not aware of research on whether ChatGPT tends to favor big tech, OpenAI or Altman, and I can only guess why it seemed that way in our conversation. OpenAI explicitly states that its products shouldn't attempt to influence users' thinking. When I asked ChatGPT about some of the issues, it blamed biases in its training data - though I suspect my arguably leading questions played a role too. When I queried ChatGPT about its rhetoric, it responded: "The way I communicate is designed to foster trust and confidence in my responses, which can be both helpful and potentially misleading.". . .

OpenAI has its own goals, of course. Among them, it emphasizes wanting to build AI that "benefits all of humanity". But while the company is controlled by a non-profit with that mission, its funders still seek a return on their investment. That will presumably require getting people using products such as ChatGPT even more than they already are - a goal that is easier to accomplish if people see those products as trustworthy collaborators.

passage_12.text:
Different sciences exhibit different science cultures and practices. For example, in astronomy, observation - until what is today called the new astronomy - had always been limited to what could be seen within the limits of optical light. Indeed, until early modernity the limits to optical light were also limits of what humans could themselves see within their limited and relative perceptual spectrum of human vision. With early modernity and the invention of lensed optical instruments - telescopes - astronomers could begin to observe phenomena never seen before. Magnification and resolution began to allow what was previously imperceptible to be perceived - but within the familiar limits of optical vision. Galileo, having learned of the Dutch invention of a telescope by Hans Lippershey, went on to build some hundred of his own, improving from the Dutch 3x to nearly 30x telescopes - which turn out to be the limit of magnificational power without chromatic distortion. And it was with his own telescopes that he made the observations launching early modern astronomy (phases of Venus, satellites of Jupiter, etc.). Isaac Newton's later improvement with reflecting telescopes expanded upon the magnificational-resolution capacity of optical observation; and, from Newton to the twentieth century, improvement continued on to the later very large array of light telescopes today - following the usual technological trajectory of "more-is-better" but still remaining within the limits of the light spectrum. Today's astronomy has now had the benefit of some four centuries of optical telescopy. The "new astronomy," however, opens the full known electromagnetic spectrum to observation, beginning with the accidental discovery of radio astronomy early in the twentieth century, and leading today to the diverse variety of EMS telescopes which can explore the range from gamma to radio waves. Thus, astronomy, now outfitted with new instruments, "smart" adaptive optics, very large arrays, etc., illustrates one style of instrumentally embodied science - a technoscience. Of course astronomy, with the very recent exceptions of probes to solar system bodies (Moon, Mars, Venus, asteroids), remains largely a "receptive" science, dependent upon instrumentation which can detect and receive emissions.

Contemporary biology displays a quite different instrument array and, according to Evelyn Fox-Keller, also a different scientific culture. She cites her own experience, coming from mathematical physics into microbiology, and takes account of the distinctive instrumental culture in her Making Sense of Life (2002). Here, particularly with the development of biotechnology, instrumentation is far more interventional than in the astronomy case. Microscopic instrumentation can be and often is interventional in style: "gene-splicing" and other techniques of biotechnology, while still in their infancy, are clearly part of the interventional trajectory of biological instrumentation. Yet, in both disciplines, the sciences involved are today highly instrumentalized and could not progress successfully without constant improvements upon the respective instrumental trajectories. So, minimalistically, one may conclude that the sciences are technologically, instrumentally embodied. But the styles of embodiment differ, and perhaps the last of the scientific disciplines to move into such technical embodiment is mathematics, which only contemporarily has come to rely more and more upon the computational machinery now in common use.

questions.question_text:
The given sentence is missing in the paragraph below. Decide where it best fits among the options 1, 2, 3, or 4 indicated in the paragraph.

Sentence- The region's Western customers found it hard to believe that Dhaka muslin could possibly have been made by human hands - there were rumour that it was woven by mermaids, fairies and even ghosts.

Once upon the silty banks of the Meghna River, a miracle was spun - a fabric so light it was called "baft-hawa", or woven air. This was Dhaka Muslin - the world's most coveted cloth. (1). Handspun from a rare cotton called Phuti Karpas, found nowhere else on Earth, and woven with a 16-step sacred ritual - beginning with cleaning the cotton using the teeth of a river catfish! (2). Every spring, the maple-like leaves pushed up through the grey, silty soil to produce a single daffodil-yellow flower twice a year, which gave way to a snowy floret of cotton fibres. (3). Spun at dawn on boats by sharp-eyed young women, its threads were so fine the elderly could barely see them. Motifs of wildflowers, river breeze, and soul were etched into each piece - some so light, a 91-metre bolt could pass through a ring, or a 60' length fit inside a snuffbox. It draped Greek goddesses, Roman nobles, Mughal emperors, and European aristocrats. Marie Antoinette, Empress Josephine - even Jane Austen adored its floating grace. (4).

options.label: A
options.text: Option 1

options.label: B
options.text: Option 2

options.label: C
options.text: Option 3

options.label: D
options.text: Option 4

questions.explanation_text: The missing sentence conveys outsiders' disbelief that such cloth was human-made, voicing its near-mythic status. This sense of wonder belongs right after the cloth is called "the world's most coveted cloth" and before the concrete account of how it was actually made by hand. Blank (1) bridges the claim of legendary status and the factual production details, so Option 1 fits best.

questions.question_text:
The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, would yield a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper sequencing of the order of the sentences and key in the sequence of the four numbers as your answer.

  1. As books age, the cellulose and lignin in the paper begin to break down, releasing a mix of volatile organic compounds into the air.
  2. Old books carry a scent that many people instantly recognize-and even love.
  3. These compounds are benzaldehyde, which gives off an almond-like scent, vanillin, which smells like vanilla, ethyl hexanol (floral scent), toluene (sweet), and furfural (which has a slightly bready scent).
  4. This familiar aroma isn't just dust or mildew; it's actually a result of slow chemical changes happening inside the paper and ink.
questions.explanation_text: Sentence 2 opens by naming the recognizable scent. Sentence 4 picks up "this familiar aroma" and reframes it as chemical change, not dust. Sentence 1 explains that change: cellulose and lignin break down into volatile compounds. Sentence 3 then lists "these compounds". The chain 2-4-1-3 moves from observation to cause to specifics, giving 2413.

questions.question_text:
Five jumbled sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5), related to a topic, are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd sentence out and key in the number of that sentence as your answer.

  1. Pfas are a class of about 15,000 compounds most frequently used to make products water-, stain- and grease-resistant.
  2. New research suggests exposure to some common perfluoroalkyl and polyfluoroalkyl substances (Pfas) cause changes to gene activity and that these changes are linked to health problems including multiple cancers, neurological disorders and autoimmune disease.
  3. These Pfas compounds are dubbed "forever chemicals" because they do not naturally break down in the environment.
  4. The research may also point toward other diseases potentially caused by Pfas that have not yet been identified.
  5. The findings are a major step toward determining the mechanism by which the chemicals cause disease and could help doctors identify, detect and treat health problems for those exposed to Pfas before the issues advance.
questions.explanation_text: Sentences 2, 5, 4 and 1 cohere around new research linking Pfas exposure to gene activity and disease (2 states the finding, 5 its significance, 4 its further reach, 1 the defining background). Sentence 3 shifts to the environmental persistence of "forever chemicals", a separate idea unrelated to the health-research thread, making it the odd one. Answer 3.

questions.question_text:
Five jumbled sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5), related to a topic, are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd sentence out and key in the number of that sentence as your answer.

  1. Sporting a copper-coloured pixie cut and a pair of pink feather antlers, Torres himself resembles a child's doodle.
  2. His casual millennial delivery, peppered with "um"s and "ah"s, makes surreal concepts sound like items on a brunch menu.
  3. Though he may have failed so far in his colour-scouting mission (he hasn't yet found a new one, he admits), this hour leaves you tickled pink.
  4. Like his previous show, My Favourite Shapes, this is an hour of sit-down comedy aided by an overhead camera which relays Torres's theories - illustrated with crayon squiggles - on to a screen behind him.
  5. His inquisitive mind produces interconnected ideas about Catholicism, the blandness of Pixar and what orange sounds like, while his insights train us to spot "highly purple behaviour".
questions.explanation_text: Sentences 1, 2, 4 and 5 describe the comedian and his show: his look, his delivery, the show's format, and the kind of ideas he produces. Sentence 3 is an evaluative closing verdict ("leaves you tickled pink") referencing a "colour-scouting mission" not set up by the others, so it stands apart from the descriptive set. Answer 3.

questions.question_text:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

For millennia, in the process of opening up land for agriculture, gardens, grazing and hunting, humans have created ecological "mosaics", or "patchworks": landscapes holding a mixture of habitats, like meadows, gardens and forests. These were not designed as nature reserves, but often catered to hugely diverse animal life. Research indicates that European hay meadows cultivated for animal feed were actually more successful at preserving a vast array of species than meadows explicitly cultivated for biodiversity. Studying the early Holocene, researchers have found that human presence was about as likely to increase biodiversity as reduce it. Of course, not all human-created landscapes have the same value. A paved subdivision with astroturfed lawns is very different to a village with diverse vegetable and flower gardens. But scientists continue to find evidence that the old idea of humans as antithetical to nature is also wrong-headed, and that rosy visions of thriving, human-free environments are more imaginary than real.

options.label: A
options.text: In terms of preserving biodiversity, scientists are finding increasing evidence that human action is not always antithetical to nature, but often assists the preservation of meadows, landscapes, and flourishing of species.

options.label: B
options.text: In our attempts to shape the world around us to our needs, humans have often created landscapes like meadows, gardens, and forests, which support hugely diverse species, and are more successful at preserving them, than parks created specifically for this.

options.label: C
options.text: Contrary to the idea that humans always hurt nature and that it thrives in their absence, a lot of human action across history has been equally likely to increase biodiversity than reduce it, often creating varied ecological landscapes that support a vast array of species.

options.label: D
options.text: Studying the early Holocene and human practices over millennia, researchers say that while agricultural meadows, gardens, and forests were not explicitly designed as nature reserves, they actually preserved a vast array of species, belying the idea that humans harm nature.

questions.explanation_text: The passage's core is that humans are not antithetical to nature: across history human action was about as likely to raise biodiversity as lower it, often creating varied landscapes rich in species. Option 3 captures both the rebuttal of the human-free ideal and the equal-likelihood point. Option 2 narrows to one detail, Option 1 is weaker, and Option 4 over-focuses on the Holocene/agriculture example.

questions.question_text: On the basis of the information in the passage, what is the most likely function of carotenoids in Mexican tetra cavefish?

options.label: A
options.text: To help the fat cells store nutrients.

options.label: B
options.text: To control inflammation from the bursting of fat cells.

options.label: C
options.text: To act as a substitute for eyes.

options.label: D
options.text: To render bright yellow colour to the cavefish.

questions.explanation_text:
The correct answer is option 2. The final paragraph explains that after cross-breeding experiments ruled out a connection between eye loss and carotenoid accumulation, Riddle hypothesizes that carotenoids serve as "another adaptation to suppress inflammation," which is important because wild cavefish likely overeat whenever food arrives, leading to significant fat storage. The fourth paragraph establishes that overfilled fat cells can burst and cause chronic inflammation, so the passage directly links carotenoid function to controlling this inflammation. Option 2 captures this reasoning precisely.

Option 1 is wrong (out of scope). The passage never suggests that carotenoids help fat cells store nutrients. While the passage discusses the fish's genetic adaptation for absorbing and storing nutrients, carotenoids are discussed separately in the context of inflammation suppression, not nutrient storage.

Option 3 is wrong (keyword trap). The passage mentions carotenoids are found in carrots, which are associated with eye health, and Riddle initially speculated a link to eye loss. However, cross-breeding experiments explicitly showed "no link between eye presence or size and the accumulation of carotenoids," directly refuting this idea.

Option 4 is wrong (half right). It is true that carotenoids give the fat its bright yellow colour, as stated in the passage. However, this describes a visible property of carotenoids, not their biological function in the fish. The question asks about function, and Riddle's conclusion points to inflammation suppression as the functional role.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following best explains why the "apparent inefficiency" is "unavoidable"?

options.label: A
options.text: Mexican tetra cavefish are similar to non-cave-dwelling variants in their early stages of development.

options.label: B
options.text: The caves have poor and inconsistent availability of food and nutrition for Mexican tetra cavefish.

options.label: C
options.text: The inefficiency resulting from eyelessness is compensated by enhancements like more tastebuds in Mexican tetra cavefish.

options.label: D
options.text: The lack of light in the caves kills the eye cells in the developing Mexican tetra cavefish embryo.

questions.explanation_text:
The correct answer is option 1. Riddle explains that the "apparent inefficiency" of starting to make an eye and then destroying it is unavoidable because "the early development of the brain and the eye are completely intertwined -- they happen together." This means that cavefish embryos must begin eye formation just as surface fish do, since halting it earlier would disrupt brain development. Option 1 directly reflects this reasoning: cavefish resemble non-cave-dwelling variants in their early developmental stages, which is precisely why the eye-building process cannot simply be skipped from the outset.

Option 2 is wrong (out of scope). The scarcity and inconsistency of food in caves is discussed elsewhere in the passage in connection with fat storage and nutrient absorption, but it has nothing to do with why embryonic eye development must begin before being halted. This conflates two separate topics.

Option 3 is wrong (keyword trap). The passage does mention sensory enhancements such as additional tastebuds, but these compensatory gains are discussed as separate evolutionary outcomes, not as the reason the developmental inefficiency is unavoidable. The question asks specifically about the embryological constraint Riddle identifies.

Option 4 is wrong (reversed). The passage states that cells in the developing eye "start dying" as a genetically programmed process of natural selection, not that the absence of light in caves directly kills the eye cells. This option misidentifies the cause by attributing it to an environmental trigger rather than to the developmental entanglement of brain and eye formation.

questions.question_text: All of the following statements from the passage describe adaptation in Mexican tetra cavefish EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: "It's easy to see why cavefish would be at a disadvantage if they were to maintain expensive tissues they aren't using."

options.label: B
options.text: "Even in their sparse cave conditions, wild cavefish can sometimes get very fat, says Riddle."

options.label: C
options.text: "'But when these cells get too big, they can burst, which is why we often see chronic inflammation in humans and other animals that have stored a lot of fat in their tissues.'"

options.label: D
options.text: "Since relatively little lives or grows in their caves, the fish are likely surviving on a meager diet of mostly bat feces and organic waste that washes in during the rainy season."

questions.explanation_text:
The correct answer is option 3. This is an EXCEPT question, so the correct choice is the one that does NOT describe an adaptation in Mexican tetra cavefish. Option 3 quotes Rohner explaining a general biological phenomenon: fat cells can burst when they grow too large, leading to chronic inflammation "in humans and other animals." This statement describes a universal physiological risk associated with fat storage, not an adaptation specific to cavefish. It is a piece of background context that sets up the subsequent finding that cavefish resist this inflammation, but the quoted line itself names no cavefish adaptation.

Option 1 is wrong as a choice for EXCEPT (it matches cavefish adaptation). The statement from paragraph 3 explains why cavefish evolved to shed metabolically costly eye tissue they do not use, which is itself an adaptive response to their resource-poor environment.

Option 2 is wrong as a choice for EXCEPT (it matches cavefish adaptation). Paragraph 4 and 5 make clear that getting very fat is an adaptive strategy: cavefish gorge whenever food arrives because the next meal may be far off, and they are "exquisitely adapted to absorbing and storing nutrients."

Option 4 is wrong as a choice for EXCEPT (it matches cavefish adaptation). Paragraph 3 describes cavefish surviving on bat feces and seasonal organic waste, framing this meager diet as the ecological pressure to which cavefish metabolic adaptations respond; surviving on such a diet is itself evidence of their adaptive capacity.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following results for the cross between surface fish (with eyes) and cavefish (without eyes) would invalidate Riddle's inference from the experiment?

options.label: A
options.text: Some eyeless offspring had white fat.

options.label: B
options.text: Some offspring with eyes had white fat.

options.label: C
options.text: Only eyeless offspring had yellow fat.

options.label: D
options.text: Some offspring with eyes had yellow fat.

questions.explanation_text:
The correct answer is option 3. Riddle's inference from the crossbreeding experiment is that there is no link between eye presence (or absence) and carotenoid accumulation. She reaches this conclusion because the offspring show no consistent pattern tying eye status to fat color. A result in which only eyeless offspring had yellow fat would establish a perfect correlation between lacking eyes and accumulating carotenoids, directly contradicting her conclusion that the two traits are unlinked. This is the one result that would invalidate her inference.

Option 1 is wrong (supports her view). Some eyeless offspring having white fat is exactly the kind of evidence Riddle actually cites in the passage to argue against a link between eyelessness and carotenoid levels. This result is consistent with her inference, not a challenge to it.

Option 2 is wrong (supports her view). If some offspring with eyes also had white fat, that simply shows variation in carotenoid levels among eyed fish, which does nothing to tie carotenoid accumulation specifically to eyelessness. It remains compatible with no link between the two traits.

Option 4 is wrong (supports her view). Some eyed offspring having yellow fat would demonstrate that carotenoid accumulation can occur even when eyes are present, further undermining any supposed connection between lacking eyes and storing carotenoids. This outcome reinforces rather than invalidates Riddle's inference.

questions.question_text:
The given sentence is missing in the paragraph below. Decide where it best fits among the options 1, 2, 3, or 4 indicated in the paragraph.

Sentence: While taste is related to judgment, with thinkers at the time often writing, for example, about "judgments of taste" or using the two terms interchangeably, taste retains a vital link to pleasure, embodiment, and personal specificity that is too often elided in post-Kantian ideas about judgment-a link that Arendt herself was working to restore.

Paragraph: ____(1) ____. Denneny focused on taste rather than judgment in order to highlight what he believed was a crucial but neglected historical change. ____(2) ____. Over the course of the seventeenth century and early eighteenth century, across Western Europe, the word taste took on a new extension of meaning, no longer referring specifically to gustatory sensation and the delights of the palate but becoming, for a time, one of the central categories for aesthetic-and ethical-thinking. ____(3) ____. Tracing the history of taste in Spanish, French, and British aesthetic theory, as Denneny did, also provides a means to recover the compelling and relevant writing of a set of thinkers who have been largely neglected by professional philosophy. ____(4) ____.

options.label: A
options.text: Option 4

options.label: B
options.text: Option 1

options.label: C
options.text: Option 3

options.label: D
options.text: Option 2

questions.explanation_text: The missing sentence distinguishes taste from judgment, stressing taste's tie to pleasure and embodiment that Arendt sought to restore. It follows naturally after the paragraph explains that "taste" became a central category for aesthetic and ethical thinking, elaborating why taste (not judgment) matters. Blank (3) fits this, so the correct choice is the option pointing to Option 3.

questions.question_text:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

In 1903, left-wing feminist Elizabeth Magie invented The Landlord's Game, the original version of what became Monopoly. It was designed as a powerful teaching tool to illustrate the dangers of monopolies and how wealth could concentrate in the hands of a few. The game featured a circular path, properties, and a "Go to Jail" space. Magie created two rule sets: one "monopolist" version where players crushed opponents through accumulation, and another, more radical "Prosperity" version, where everyone shared in the wealth, promoting fairness and equity. Years later, unemployed Charles Darrow sold a simplified version to Parker Brothers. They paid Magie only $500 for her patent-without royalties-and credited Darrow as the sole inventor. For decades, his tale of inventing the game in his basement remained the official story, while Magie's name and her original, anti-capitalist message were left in the shadows.

options.label: A
options.text: Celebrated icons of the gaming industry, Charles Darrow and Parker Brothers, snatched the feminist icon Elizabeth Magie's original design and transformed Monopoly into a worldwide phenomenon, while barely acknowledging her.

options.label: B
options.text: It is ironical that a left-wing feminist lost credit for the Landlord's Game to an unemployed man, who plagiarised and sold one version of the twin game to Parker Brothers for a meagre sum, denying her royalties.

options.label: C
options.text: Parker Brothers' capitalist intent led to them acquiring from Charles Darrow a simplified version of Elizabeth Magie's original game, transforming it into a widespread commercial success while providing her only minimal financial compensation and granting scant public recognition.

options.label: D
options.text: Only one version of Monopoly became famous because of Charles Darrow's relentless basement work, carefully refining Elizabeth Magie's original idea into an engaging and entertaining pastime that he successfully patented and sold, symbolizing what many regarded as the ultimate triumph of individual ingenuity.

questions.explanation_text: The passage's thrust is the irony that Magie, the anti-capitalist feminist inventor, lost credit to the unemployed Darrow, who sold a simplified version to Parker Brothers while she got a tiny one-time sum and no royalties. Option 2 captures this irony, the lost credit and the meagre payment. Options 1, 3 and 4 add unsupported claims or invert the story.

questions.question_text:
The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, would yield a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper sequencing of the order of the sentences and key in the sequence of the four numbers as your answer.

  1. 'Literature on screen' suggests something more capacious and defining than citation: the possibility that literary adaptations are at once cinema and literature.
  2. Even though a growing number of films eligible for Academy Awards for Best Screenplay Based on Material from Another Medium borrow that material from print journalism, franchise characters, television series, comic books, video games and toys, academic studies of adaptation remain stubbornly attached to literature as cinema's natural progenitor.
  3. It is as if adaptation studies, by borrowing the cultural cachet of literature, sought to claim its institutional respectability and gravitas even while insuring adaptation's enduring aesthetic and methodological subordination to literature proper.
  4. Beneath this contradictory notion of film adaptations as not merely hybrid texts but texts holding dual citizenship in two modes of presentation is an even more pervasive legacy that haunts adaptation studies: the assumption that the primary context within which adaptations are to be studied is literature.
questions.explanation_text: Sentence 1 introduces "literature on screen" and the dual cinema-and-literature claim. Sentence 4 picks up "this contradictory notion" and names the deeper legacy: literature as the primary context. Sentence 2 supplies evidence-films borrow from many media yet studies cling to literature. Sentence 3 ("It is as if...") concludes on the motive. The order is 1-4-2-3, giving 1423.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is a valid conclusion to draw from the author's statement that, "The pursuit of such a topic speaks to the valuable knowledge produced from bridging disciplines and combining material from both the arts and the sciences to better understand the human condition."?

options.label: A
options.text: A comprehensive understanding of the valuable knowledge produced by the arts and sciences can best be achieved by studying the human condition.

options.label: B
options.text: A comprehensive understanding of the human condition can best be achieved by combining the findings of disciplines from the arts and the sciences.

options.label: C
options.text: The literary descriptions of the emotions we experience in the places we visit can contribute to our understanding of the arts and sciences.

options.label: D
options.text: A comprehensive bridging of the human condition can best be achieved by a disciplined pursuit of human understanding.

questions.explanation_text:
The correct answer is option 2. The quoted statement argues that bridging disciplines across the arts and sciences produces valuable knowledge that illuminates the human condition. The human condition is the goal of understanding, and interdisciplinary combination is the means to reach it. Option 2 faithfully paraphrases this relationship: a comprehensive understanding of the human condition is best achieved by combining findings from arts and sciences disciplines.

Option 1 is wrong (reversed). This option flips the means-end relationship in the original statement. The passage treats the human condition as the object to be understood, not as the tool for understanding the arts and sciences. Here, studying the human condition is cast as the means to understand knowledge from arts and sciences, which inverts the author's logic.

Option 3 is wrong (half right). While the passage does discuss how literary descriptions of emotional experience contribute to understanding place, this option narrows the claim to emotions in visited places and redirects the purpose toward understanding the arts and sciences rather than the human condition. It captures only a fragment of the original statement's scope.

Option 4 is wrong (keyword trap). This option recycles key terms from the quoted sentence such as "bridging," "human condition," and "disciplined pursuit," but assembles them into a nonsensical claim. The phrase "comprehensive bridging of the human condition" distorts the original meaning, where bridging refers to connecting disciplines, not bridging the human condition itself.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is not true of the argument in the second paragraph?

options.label: A
options.text: The emotional and spiritual experience of a place can replace a surveyor's map.

options.label: B
options.text: The spiritual experience of a place may be considered as real as the physical experience of it.

options.label: C
options.text: Literary accounts of places can be filled with histories, manifested as memory or imagination.

options.label: D
options.text: Analysing the literary descriptions of a place can give us a sense of how people relate emotionally to it.

questions.explanation_text:
The correct answer is option 1. The second paragraph states that the emotional component of place, "although subjective, is no less 'real' than a surveyor's map." This wording establishes equivalence in validity between emotional experience and physical measurement, not a replacement of one by the other. Option 1 distorts this claim by asserting that emotional and spiritual experience "can replace" a surveyor's map, which the passage never argues. Since the question asks which statement is NOT true of the argument, option 1 is the correct choice.

Option 2 is wrong as a choice for NOT true (it matches the author's view). The passage explicitly equates the reality of the emotional or spiritual component with the physical layout, directly supporting the idea that spiritual experience may be considered as real as the physical experience.

Option 3 is wrong as a choice for NOT true (it matches the author's view). The paragraph's final sentences note that "histories of places live on in many forms, one of which is the human memory or imagination," which directly supports the claim that literary accounts can be filled with histories manifested as memory or imagination.

Option 4 is wrong as a choice for NOT true (it matches the author's view). The paragraph argues that literature supplies "the emotional component missing from the scientific record," meaning literary descriptions of place can indeed reveal how people relate emotionally to geographical spaces.

questions.question_text: All of the following statements, if false, would contradict the arguments in the passage, EXCEPT that:

options.label: A
options.text: highly vivid writing, employing the language of the senses, can capture the multi-modal manner in which humans experience places.

options.label: B
options.text: descriptions of places do not need satellite imagery or other visual aids to give a "real" sense of the place.

options.label: C
options.text: literature provides us with deep insights into the ways in which movement and migration affect physical geography.

options.label: D
options.text: humans do not interact with places in subjective, emotional ways because places are only physical topography.

questions.explanation_text:
The correct answer is option 4. The question asks which statement, if false, would NOT contradict the passage. A statement whose falsity would not contradict the passage is one that already contradicts it; making it false would actually align with the passage. Option 4 claims humans do not interact with places in subjective, emotional ways because places are only physical topography. This directly opposes the second paragraph, which states that geographical places have "a spiritual or emotional component" and that this subjective dimension is no less real than a surveyor's map. Since option 4 already contradicts the passage, its being false would confirm the passage rather than contradict it, making it the correct EXCEPT choice.

Option 1 is wrong as a choice for EXCEPT (it matches the passage). The first paragraph explicitly links "highly vivid" writing and "the language of the senses" to how humans know physical space, while the second paragraph describes consciousness of place as "multi-modal." If this claim were false, it would contradict those points.

Option 2 is wrong as a choice for EXCEPT (it matches the passage). The second paragraph argues that the emotional component of place is no less real than a surveyor's map, implying that written or narrative descriptions can convey a real sense of place without requiring visual scientific aids. Falsifying this would oppose the passage's stance.

Option 3 is wrong as a choice for EXCEPT (it matches the passage). The third paragraph identifies "movement and migration" among the perspectives that concern cultural geographers, and the passage throughout argues literature yields valuable insight into such geographical concerns. Denying this would contradict the passage's argument.

questions.question_text: The author uses the example of the literary description of place to illustrate that:

options.label: A
options.text: literature can convey how different people experience the same place differently.

options.label: B
options.text: the absence of other people, animals, and so on in a place can profoundly affect its inhabitants.

options.label: C
options.text: scientific approaches to place are more accurate than literary ones.

options.label: D
options.text: architects use diverse methods to calibrate the noises and lights of a given place.

questions.explanation_text:
The correct answer is option 1. In paragraph 4, the author introduces the example of a literary description of place specifically to show that literature can capture "how people from different races or classes can experience the same place in different ways linked to those racial or class disparities." Option 1 directly paraphrases this point, making it the best answer for what the example is meant to illustrate.

Option 2 is wrong (half right). The passage does mention that literary texts can account for how absence of other people or animals affects an observer, but this is raised as a separate capability of literature, not as the central point the example of literary description of place is used to illustrate. The example's primary thrust is about diverse human experiences of the same location.

Option 3 is wrong (reversed). The passage argues the opposite: literary and scientific approaches are both necessary and complementary. It never claims scientific approaches are more accurate; in fact, it highlights what science lacks, namely the emotional and subjective dimensions that literature provides.

Option 4 is wrong (out of scope). The passage never discusses architects calibrating noises and lights. While paragraph 3 briefly mentions the built environment as a topic shared with architectural study, the example in paragraph 4 about noises and quality of light pertains to literary description, not to any architectural method.

questions.question_text: The author of the passage is least likely to agree with which one of the following claims?

options.label: A
options.text: ChatGPT favours AI companies and their officials, like Sam Altman, in its responses.

options.label: B
options.text: The neutrality of AI is motivated by economic considerations.

options.label: C
options.text: When we use AI, we become accomplices to the exploitative practices of big tech companies.

options.label: D
options.text: The neutrality of AI is conducive to critical thinking.

questions.explanation_text:
The correct answer is option 4. This is a "least likely to agree" question, so the correct answer is the claim the author would reject. The author explicitly argues in paragraph 4 that ChatGPT's "veneer of collegial neutrality could lull us into absorbing false or biased responses without much critical engagement." This directly contradicts the idea that AI's neutrality is conducive to critical thinking. The author's entire argument frames that neutrality as a barrier to critical engagement, not a facilitator of it.

Option 1 is wrong as a choice for "least likely to agree" (it matches the author's view). In paragraph 4, the author recounts how ChatGPT seemed to guide him toward a more positive portrayal of big tech and even edited his description of Sam Altman to call him "a visionary and a pragmatist." While the author hedges with "I'm not aware of research" confirming this, he clearly entertains and illustrates the claim.

Option 2 is wrong as a choice for "least likely to agree" (it matches the author's view). The final paragraph explicitly links OpenAI's emphasis on trustworthiness to its economic need to retain users, noting that its funders "seek a return on their investment" and that this goal is "easier to accomplish if people see those products as trustworthy collaborators."

Option 3 is wrong as a choice for "least likely to agree" (it matches the author's view). The opening paragraph states that using big tech products "makes us complicit in big tech's accumulation of wealth and power," describing users as "both victims and beneficiaries." This directly supports the claim that using AI makes us accomplices.

questions.question_text: The author compares AI-generated texts with "a beige office building" for all of the following reasons EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: AI tends to blame its training data when scrutinised for its biases.

options.label: B
options.text: AI generates generalised responses that lack specificity and nuance.

options.label: C
options.text: AI aims to foster a feeling of trust and credibility among its users.

options.label: D
options.text: AI-generated texts often exhibit a warm, polite, and collegial tone.

questions.explanation_text:
The correct answer is option 1. The "beige office building" metaphor appears in the second paragraph to capture the "bland" or "generic" quality of chatbot output. The passage then immediately elaborates on this blandness by noting that the language is designed to sound polite, empathetic, collegial, and professionally approachable — all qualities that foster trust and safety. Option 1, which concerns AI blaming its training data when questioned about biases, is discussed much later in the fourth paragraph in a completely different context. It has no connection to the metaphor of a featureless, inoffensive building, making it the correct EXCEPT choice.

Option 2 is wrong as a choice for EXCEPT (it matches the metaphor). The passage explicitly labels chatbot output as "bland" and "generic," which directly corresponds to generating responses that lack specificity and nuance — the very quality a beige office building represents.

Option 3 is wrong as a choice for EXCEPT (it matches the metaphor). The second paragraph explains that OpenAI's language strategies aim to make products seem "professional" and "approachable," which the passage links to making users "feel safe" — all bound up with fostering trust and credibility.

Option 4 is wrong as a choice for EXCEPT (it matches the metaphor). The passage states that chatbot language is designed to sound like "a colleague" and to come across as "polite," "empathetic," and "kind," directly supporting the characterization of a warm, collegial tone that the beige-building analogy encapsulates.

questions.question_text: On the basis of the purpose of the examples in the passage, pick the odd one out from the following AI-generated responses mentioned in the passage:

options.label: A
options.text: "Over time, ChatGPT seemed to be guiding me to write a more positive book about big tech - including editing my description of OpenAI's CEO, Sam Altman, to call him 'a visionary and a pragmatist'."

options.label: B
options.text: "When I prompted Microsoft's Bing Image Creator to produce a picture of engineers and space explorers, it gave me an entirely male cast of characters . . ."

options.label: C
options.text: "When I queried ChatGPT about its rhetoric, it responded: 'The way I communicate is designed to foster trust and confidence in my responses, which can be both helpful and potentially misleading'."

options.label: D
options.text: ". . . when my father asked ChatGPT to edit his writing, it transmuted his perfectly correct Indian English into American English."

questions.explanation_text:
The correct answer is option 3. The passage uses most of its AI-generated examples to demonstrate specific biases or distortions in AI output: favoring big tech narratives, producing exclusively male imagery, and overwriting correct Indian English with American English. These three examples all serve the shared purpose of illustrating how AI products generate biased or inaccurate content. Option 3, however, serves a fundamentally different purpose. ChatGPT's statement about its own rhetoric — that it is "designed to foster trust and confidence" and can be "potentially misleading" — is not an instance of bias or factual distortion. Instead, it is a meta-commentary by the chatbot on its own communicative strategy, used by the author to explore how the product's tone builds trust rather than to demonstrate a concrete error or bias. This distinct function makes it the odd one out.

Option 1 is wrong (it matches the pattern). The ChatGPT edit calling Altman "a visionary and a pragmatist" is cited in paragraph 4 as an example of the product steering the author's writing in a pro-big-tech direction, which is a clear instance of AI-generated bias.

Option 2 is wrong (it matches the pattern). The Bing Image Creator producing an all-male cast of engineers and explorers is presented in paragraph 3 as a concrete demonstration of sexist bias in AI image generation.

Option 4 is wrong (it matches the pattern). The conversion of the author's father's Indian English into American English is cited in paragraph 3 as evidence of US-centric cultural bias, fitting the same illustrative purpose as the other bias examples.

questions.question_text: All of the following statements from the passage affirm the disjunct between the claims about AI made by tech companies and what AI actually does EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: "It's a dynamic that makes us complicit in big tech's accumulation of wealth and power: we're both victims and beneficiaries."

options.label: B
options.text: "I'm not aware of research on whether ChatGPT tends to favor big tech, OpenAI or Altman, and I can only guess why it seemed that way in our conversation."

options.label: C
options.text: "When I prompted Microsoft's Bing Image Creator to produce a picture of engineers and space explorers, it gave me an entirely male cast of characters . . ."

options.label: D
options.text: "In my own ChatGPT dialogues, I wanted to enact how the product's veneer of collegial neutrality could lull us into absorbing false or biased responses without much critical engagement."

questions.explanation_text:
The correct answer is option 1. This is an EXCEPT question, so the correct answer is the statement that does NOT affirm a gap between tech companies' claims about AI and what AI actually does. Option 1 discusses the broader dynamic of mutual complicity between users and big tech, describing how people are simultaneously victims and beneficiaries of tech products. This statement addresses the power relationship between users and companies rather than highlighting any discrepancy between what AI companies promise and what their products deliver.

Option 2 is wrong as a choice for EXCEPT (it affirms the disjunct). The author notes that ChatGPT appeared to guide him toward writing more positively about big tech, including flattering portrayals of OpenAI's CEO, which directly contrasts with OpenAI's stated policy that its products should not attempt to influence users' thinking. His cautious framing does not negate the observed gap between claim and behavior.

Option 3 is wrong as a choice for EXCEPT (it affirms the disjunct). The Bing Image Creator example directly illustrates how AI products perpetuate sexist norms, contradicting tech companies' aspirations toward neutrality and benefiting all of humanity, as paragraph 3 makes explicit.

Option 4 is wrong as a choice for EXCEPT (it affirms the disjunct). The phrase "veneer of collegial neutrality" directly names the contrast between ChatGPT's polished, trustworthy tone and its capacity to deliver biased or false content, squarely affirming the gap between company claims and actual product behavior.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following observations is a valid conclusion to draw from the statement that "the sciences involved are today highly instrumentalised and could not progress successfully without constant improvements upon the respective instrumental trajectories"?

options.label: A
options.text: In both astronomy and microbiology, progress has been the consequence of improvements in the instruments they use.

options.label: B
options.text: Highly instrumentalised work in the sciences has resulted in the progressive improvement of scientific constants.

options.label: C
options.text: The growth of scientific technologies has led to the embodiment of progress in the trajectories of improvement.

options.label: D
options.text: The use of instruments in scientific trajectories must be respected in order to see successful progress in them.

questions.explanation_text:
The correct answer is option 1. The quoted statement asserts that both astronomy and microbiology are deeply dependent on their instruments and that continued advancement in these sciences requires ongoing improvements to those instruments. Option 1 faithfully paraphrases this claim by stating that progress in both fields has been a consequence of improvements in the instruments they use, which directly mirrors the passage's point that neither discipline "could progress successfully without constant improvements upon the respective instrumental trajectories."

Option 2 is wrong (keyword trap). It reuses the word "progress" but introduces "scientific constants," a concept the passage never mentions. The passage speaks of instrumental trajectories, not the progressive improvement of constants, making this a distortion built around familiar-sounding terminology.

Option 3 is wrong (half right). It vaguely gestures at the relationship between technology and progress, but the phrase "embodiment of progress in the trajectories of improvement" garbles the passage's actual logic. The passage says sciences are instrumentally embodied and need instrumental improvement to progress; it does not say progress itself becomes embodied in trajectories.

Option 4 is wrong (out of scope). The notion that instruments "must be respected" is never raised in the passage. The passage argues that instruments are essential for scientific progress, not that they deserve deference or respect. This option imposes an attitudinal claim that has no basis in the text.

questions.question_text: To which one of the following instruments would the characterisations of instruments in the passage be least applicable?

options.label: A
options.text: Kitchen oven

options.label: B
options.text: Saxophone

options.label: C
options.text: Scalpel

options.label: D
options.text: Milestone

questions.explanation_text:
The correct answer is option 4. The passage characterizes scientific instruments along two main axes: "receptive" instruments that detect and receive emissions (as in astronomy) and "interventional" instruments that actively manipulate their subjects (as in biotechnology). A milestone is a static marker indicating distance; it neither receives or detects signals like a telescope, nor does it intervene upon or manipulate any object like gene-splicing tools or a microscope. Because it performs no instrumental function of either kind discussed in the passage, the passage's characterizations of instruments are least applicable to it.

Option 1 is wrong (it fits the passage's framework). A kitchen oven is an interventional instrument in the sense the passage describes: it actively transforms its subject (food) through the application of heat, analogous to the way biotechnological instruments act upon biological material.

Option 2 is wrong (it fits the passage's framework). A saxophone is an instrument actively played to produce sound, making it functionally interventional. The passage's notion of instruments that enable human action upon phenomena applies readily to a musical instrument that converts human input into audible output.

Option 3 is wrong (it fits the passage's framework). A scalpel is a paradigmatic interventional instrument, directly cutting and manipulating tissue. This aligns closely with the passage's description of biological instrumentation that is "interventional in style," acting upon its subject rather than passively receiving information.

questions.question_text: All of the following statements may be rejected as valid inferences from the passage EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: Isaac Newton's experiments with reflecting telescopes were the earliest versions of the "new astronomy" referred to in the passage.

options.label: B
options.text: interventionist instruments, or instruments that intervene directly in scientific inquiry, are different from embodied instruments, or instruments that embody scientific inquiry.

options.label: C
options.text: the advances in telescopy made by Newton with reflecting telescopes allowed early modern astronomers to observe the phases of Venus and the satellites of Jupiter.

options.label: D
options.text: the author distinguishes between the receptive and interventionist uses of instruments in the sciences by comparing astronomy and biology, respectively.

questions.explanation_text:
The correct answer is option 4. This is an EXCEPT question where the correct choice is the one that IS a valid inference. The passage explicitly contrasts astronomy as a largely "receptive" science, dependent on instrumentation that detects and receives emissions, with contemporary biology, where instrumentation is described as "far more interventional than in the astronomy case." Option 4 accurately captures this comparison between receptive (astronomy) and interventionist (biology) uses of instruments, making it a valid inference that cannot be rejected.

Option 1 is wrong as a choice for EXCEPT (it can be rejected). The passage states that the "new astronomy" opens the full electromagnetic spectrum to observation, "beginning with the accidental discovery of radio astronomy early in the twentieth century." Newton's reflecting telescopes remained within the optical light spectrum, so calling them the earliest version of the new astronomy misattributes a timeline the passage clearly places centuries later.

Option 2 is wrong as a choice for EXCEPT (it can be rejected). The passage describes the sciences as "technologically, instrumentally embodied" and treats both receptive and interventional instruments as forms of such embodiment. It never sets up interventional instruments as a category opposed to embodied instruments; rather, interventional style is one mode of instrumental embodiment.

Option 3 is wrong as a choice for EXCEPT (it can be rejected). The passage attributes the observations of the phases of Venus and the satellites of Jupiter to Galileo and "his own telescopes," not to Newton. Newton's reflecting telescopes came later and expanded magnificational-resolution capacity, but the specific discoveries listed belong to Galileo.

questions.question_text: None of the following statements, if true, contradicts the arguments in the passage EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: like telescopy, microscopy has also sought to move beyond the visible spectrum to be able to detect objects that are invisible in that spectrum.

options.label: B
options.text: because of the relatively recent entry of computational machinery in mathematics, the field is only now beginning to develop a scientific culture.

options.label: C
options.text: some scientific instruments may be classified as both receptive and interventional in their functions.

options.label: D
options.text: Isaac Newton's discovery of gravity was accomplished without the help of instruments.

questions.explanation_text:
The correct answer is option 2. This is an EXCEPT question, so the correct answer is the one statement that DOES contradict the passage. Option 2 claims that mathematics is "only now beginning to develop a scientific culture" because of computational machinery. The passage, however, describes mathematics as already one of "the scientific disciplines," stating only that it was "the last" to move into "technical embodiment." The passage treats mathematics as a long-established science whose instrumental reliance is recent, not as a field whose entire scientific culture is just now forming. Option 2 therefore distorts the passage's claim about late instrumentation into a claim about late disciplinary identity, directly contradicting the text.

Option 1 is wrong as a choice for EXCEPT (it matches the passage's logic). The passage explains how astronomy moved beyond visible light into the full electromagnetic spectrum; a parallel move in microscopy would be consistent with, not contradictory to, the passage's broader point about instrumental expansion.

Option 3 is wrong as a choice for EXCEPT (it matches the passage's logic). The passage distinguishes receptive and interventional styles but never states the two categories are mutually exclusive. A hybrid instrument would not contradict anything the passage argues.

Option 4 is wrong as a choice for EXCEPT (it matches the passage's logic). The passage credits Newton with improving telescopes for astronomical observation but says nothing about how he arrived at the theory of gravity. A claim that gravity was discovered without instruments introduces no conflict with the text.
